title: Business
subtitle: launch a business, roll out a range, face stiff competition
summary: Talk about starting and growing a company using the words and collocations that business people really use.

lesson.heading: Starting a business
lesson.text: Ryan Archer wanted a computer that suited him exactly, so he went to his bank manager and **put forward** a **business plan** to sell **custom-built** computers on the Internet. He **launched** the business a year later, and two years after that he **rolled out** an **expanded** range of tablets and hand-held devices.

examples.note: = offered it for people to consider
= specially made for one particular person

examples.text: He **launched** the business a year later.
examples.note: = started it, often with a special event

examples.text: His **firm** now **manufactures** around 200 machines a year.
examples.note: firm = company; manufacture = produce goods in large numbers

lesson.heading: Words from Ryan's story
rows: make it available for the first time
a range that has been made bigger
something very important that must be dealt with first
finding out beforehand what people want or need (uncountable)
a period of low economic activity and bad conditions for business
people who may buy when the conditions are right
the possibility of something bad happening
the list of orders waiting to be completed
going into the future, from now on

lesson.heading: Verbs used with and without an object

left.label: with an object
left.text: Someone does the action to the product.
examples: They are **rolling out** a new range.

right.label: the product as subject
right.text: In business English the real object often becomes the subject, with no passive.
examples: We didn't know if the instruments would **sell**.
The new range will **roll out** next year.

lesson.note: Say The new range will launch next month, not ~~will launch itself~~. Say We hope it will sell, not ~~it will be sold~~.

lesson.heading: Advice from a CEO
lesson.text: The **CEO** (Chief Executive Officer) of a large **corporation** gave these tips. Notice that you **do business** in a market, **access** new markets, **make a profit** and **face stiff competition**.

examples.text: **Do business** in the markets you know best before trying to enter new ones.
It may be difficult to **access new markets**. **Build contacts**; that's the secret.
You may not **make a profit** immediately. Be patient.
You will probably **face stiff competition**, so make sure your product is the best.
Get regular **feedback** from your employees and customers.

lesson.heading: Collocations worth learning by heart
rows: Customer care should be a priority in any kind of business.
The order books were half-empty, so the company had to close down.
Market research showed that customers wanted a wider range of software.
Custom-built cars are much more expensive than ordinary ones.
The firm faced stiff competition from Chinese companies.

lesson.heading: business: countable or uncountable?

left.label: uncountable = the activity
left.text: This is trade, buying and selling in general. It has no plural.
examples: We hope to do more **business** in Asia next year.
It's not easy to do **business** during a recession.

right.label: countable = a company
right.text: Here a business is one enterprise, so it can be plural.
examples: New **businesses** are launched on the Internet every day.
She runs a small **business** in Leeds.

lesson.note: Not ~~We hope to do more businesses in Asia~~.

lesson.text: *Feedback*, *competition*, *market research* and *business* (the activity) are all uncountable - never put *a* in front of them or add *-s*.

exercises.prompt: Match the words to make typical business collocations.
What did Ryan Archer put forward to his bank manager? He presented a business ___.
exercises.explanation: A business plan sets out how the business will operate.

exercises.prompt: When did he ___ his business? A year later.
exercises.explanation: Launch a business = start it, often with an event to mark the beginning.

exercises.prompt: Why didn't he do any market research? He felt there were enough ___ customers.
exercises.explanation: Potential customers are people who may buy when the conditions are right.

exercises.prompt: Why was he not sure if the machines would sell? There was a ___ at the time.
exercises.explanation: A recession is a period of low economic activity and bad conditions for business.

exercises.prompt: We need to ___ our business in Latin America.
exercises.explanation: Expand = make bigger. The noun phrase is an expanded range.

exercises.prompt: Rewrite in business English: 'The new service will be available for the first time over the whole country next year.'
options: The new service will roll out nationally next year.
The new service will put forward nationally next year.
The new service will access nationally next year.
The new service will feedback nationally next year.
exercises.explanation: Roll out = make a new product or service available for the first time.

exercises.prompt: Rewrite in business English: 'The business didn't make money in its first year.'
options: The business didn't make a profit in its first year.
The business didn't make a priority in its first year.
The business didn't make a recession in its first year.
The business didn't make a feedback in its first year.
exercises.explanation: Make a profit is the standard collocation for earning money from a business.

exercises.prompt: It is sometimes difficult to ___ new markets if you don't have contacts.
exercises.explanation: Access a market = reach it and do business in it.

exercises.statement: She's the COE of a huge corporation.
exercises.explanation: She's the CEO of a huge corporation. CEO stands for Chief Executive Officer.

exercises.statement: We hope to do more businesses in North Africa in the future.
exercises.explanation: We hope to do more business in North Africa in the future. Business meaning trade is uncountable.

exercises.statement: It's important to get feedback from our clients.
exercises.explanation: Correct. Feedback is uncountable, so no a and no plural.

exercises.prompt: Put the sentence in order. It means 'from now on we expect our sales to grow'.
exercises.answer: Going forward, we expect to increase our sales in Japan and China.
exercises.explanation: Going forward = going into the future. Not ~~Bringing forward~~.
